title: Small generation of categorical equivalences under filtered colimits
statement: Use the small simplicial sets, quasicategories, internal functor simplicial sets and coherent natural equivalences of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention]. Use categorical equivalence in the convention of [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure]: $u:K\to L$ is a categorical equivalence when $h\operatorname{Fun}(L,C)\to h\operatorname{Fun}(K,C)$ is an equivalence of ordinary categories for every quasicategory $C$ in a sufficiently large universe; $hS$ is the category generated by its vertices and edges, with degenerate edges identified with identities and each $2$-simplex imposing the relation that its long edge is the composite of its other two edges. Let $E$ be the class of categorical equivalences between small simplicial sets. There is a small set $E_0\subseteq E$ such that every arrow in $E$ is isomorphic, in the arrow category of simplicial sets, to a small filtered colimit of arrows in $E_0$. The arrow category has maps as objects and commuting squares as morphisms; its colimits are computed at source and target. A small indexing category is filtered when every finite diagram in it, including the empty diagram, has a cocone.

source.place: Theorem 2.2.5.1, proof (1), printed p. 90, specifically condition (4) of perfectness in Definition A.2.6.12, printed p. 825; Proposition 2.2.5.8, printed pp. 94-95, identifies the ordinary hFun testing convention. Read online 2026-10-17; no Stacks tag states this result.

proof.text: Fix the input universe. Write $\mathcal S=\mathrm{sSet}$ and $\mathcal A=\mathrm{sCat}$. The simplicial-set definition identifies $\mathcal S$ with $\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Set})$, so [lem-coef-presheaf-local-presentability] makes $\mathcal S$ locally presentable. By [lem-coef-simplicial-interval-lifting], $\mathcal A$ is complete and locally presentable, and its families $I,J$ are small sets of maps. Apply the presheaf result also with indexing category $[1]^{\mathrm{op}}$ and target $\mathcal S$ or $\mathcal A$ to see that both arrow categories are locally presentable. The required pullbacks exist in $\mathcal S$ degreewise, and in $\mathcal A$ by completeness. Colimits of arrows are computed on endpoints: a cocone of squares is exactly two endpoint cocones whose induced maps commute, by the colimit universal property.

source.place: Agent derivation from the cited DAG statements; motivated by HTT Theorem 2.2.5.1, proof (1), and Corollary A.2.6.7

proof.text: Let $W$ be the Dwyer--Kan equivalences, in the convention of [lem-coef-simplicial-interval-cell-stability]. Every map in the weakly saturated closure of $J$ belongs to $W$. Indeed $J$ lies in $J\text{-cof}={}^{\square}(J\text{-inj})$ directly from the definition of $J\text{-inj}$. An isomorphism $i:X\to Y$ has the left lifting property against every map: in a square with top map $u:X\to A$, the diagonal is $ui^{-1}$. The lifting-class closure and transfinite left-lifting statements then show that $J\text{-cof}$ is closed under pushouts, transfinite compositions and arrow retracts. Thus the weakly saturated closure of $J$ is contained in $J\text{-cof}$. The interval-lifting statement makes every member of $J\text{-cof}$ a retract of a relative $J\text{-cell}$ map, and the cell-stability statement puts all such cell maps and their retracts in $W$.

source.place: Agent derivation from the cited DAG statements; motivated by HTT Theorem 2.2.5.1, proof (1), and Corollary A.2.6.7

proof.text: A functor $p:A\to B$ lies in $I\text{-inj}$ exactly when it is surjective on objects and each map $A(a,a')\to B(pa,pa')$ is a trivial Kan fibration. To check this directly, lifting against $\varnothing\to\{0\}$ is surjectivity on objects. A square against $U(\partial\Delta^n)\to U(\Delta^n)$ fixes two source objects $a,a'$ and is precisely a boundary-lifting problem for the displayed mapping-set map, also when $a=a'$. The Kan--Quillen statement identifies lifting against all boundaries, including $n=0$, with trivial Kan fibrations. Consequently every $I\text{-inj}$ functor is in $W$: its local maps are weak homotopy equivalences, hence give bijections on components and full faithfulness of $\pi_0p$, while object surjectivity gives essential surjectivity. A fully faithful essentially surjective ordinary functor is an equivalence: choose an object preimage up to isomorphism, and define its inverse on morphisms using the fully faithful Hom bijections.

source.place: Agent derivation from the cited DAG statements; motivated by HTT Theorem 2.2.5.1, proof (1), and Corollary A.2.6.7

proof.text: For $p\in J\text{-inj}$ one has $p\in W$ if and only if $p\in I\text{-inj}$. The reverse implication is step 3. In the forward direction, the interval-lifting criterion makes each local map a Kan fibration; the assumption $p\in W$ makes it also a weak homotopy equivalence, hence a trivial fibration in the Kan--Quillen model structure. For any object $b\in B$, essential surjectivity supplies $a\in A$ and an isomorphism $pa\simeq b$ in $\pi_0B$. Represent that isomorphism by a vertex of $B(pa,b)$. The equivalence-lifting clause for $J\text{-inj}$ then supplies $a'$ with $pa'=b$. Thus $p$ is surjective on objects and step 3 applies. No local fibrancy assumption on $A$ or $B$ was used.

source.place: Agent derivation from the cited DAG statements; motivated by HTT Theorem 2.2.5.1, proof (1), and Corollary A.2.6.7

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-accessible-small-object-factorization] to the locally presentable category $\mathcal A$ and the small generating set $J$. Choose its functorial factorization $f=p_f i_f$, and define $R:\mathcal A^{[1]}\to\mathcal A^{[1]}$ by $R(f)=p_f:E(f)\to\operatorname{target}(f)$. Functoriality of the factorization supplies its maps of squares. There is an infinite regular $\kappa$ for which $E$ preserves small $\kappa$-filtered colimits; since the target projection preserves all colimits and arrow colimits are computed on endpoints, $R$ preserves those colimits too. Step 2 gives $i_f\in W$; moreover $p_f\in J\text{-inj}$. By two-out-of-three for $W$ and step 4, $f\in W$ holds exactly when $R(f)\in I\text{-inj}$.

source.place: Agent derivation from the cited DAG statements; motivated by HTT Theorem 2.2.5.1, proof (1), and Corollary A.2.6.7

proof.text: Let $\mathfrak C:\mathcal S\to\mathcal A$ be the rigidification explicitly defined in [lem-coef-rigidification-equivalence-detection]. It preserves small colimits, as can be checked without a model-localization theorem. Define a simplicial set $N_A$ by $(N_A)_n=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(\mathfrak C[\Delta^n],A)$ with operators given by precomposition. A map from the defining simplex colimit to $A$ is a family of enriched functors $g_x:\mathfrak C[\Delta^n]\to A$, one for each $x\in S_n$, satisfying $g_{S(\alpha)x}=g_x\mathfrak C[\Delta(\alpha)]$ for every $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$. These are exactly the equations for the assignments $x\mapsto g_x$ to be a simplicial map $S\to N_A$. Conversely, such a simplicial map gives that compatible family and hence a unique enriched functor from the colimit. These constructions are inverse and commute with precomposition in $S$ and postcomposition in $A$, giving natural bijections $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(\mathfrak C[S],A)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal S}(S,N_A)$. For any small diagram $S_d$ with colimit $S$, maps $S\to N_A$ are compatible families $S_d\to N_A$; under the bijections these are exactly cocones of maps $\mathfrak C[S_d]\to A$. This proves the colimit universal property for $\mathfrak C[S]$. Hence the induced arrow functor $\mathfrak C^{[1]}$ preserves small colimits on both endpoints. The same rigidification criterion gives $u\in E$ exactly when $\mathfrak C[u]\in W$.

source.place: Agent derivation from the cited DAG statements; motivated by HTT Theorem 2.2.5.1, proof (1), and Corollary A.2.6.7

proof.text: By [lem-coef-small-right-lifting-accessibility], the full subcategory $\mathcal V\subseteq\mathcal A^{[1]}$ on $I\text{-inj}$ is replete and accessible: step 1 verified local presentability of $\mathcal A$ and smallness of $I$, which are all the hypotheses of that lemma. Form $H=R\circ\mathfrak C^{[1]}:\mathcal S^{[1]}\to\mathcal A^{[1]}$. Steps 5 and 6 show that it preserves small $\kappa$-filtered colimits. By steps 5 and 6, $H(u)\in\mathcal V$ if and only if $u\in E$.

source.place: Agent derivation from the cited DAG statements; motivated by HTT Theorem 2.2.5.1, proof (1), and Corollary A.2.6.7

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-accessible-full-inverse-image] to $H$ and $\mathcal V$. Both its ambient categories are locally presentable by step 1, $H$ preserves sufficiently filtered colimits by step 7, and $\mathcal V$ is replete accessible by step 7. Its conclusion says that the full subcategory on $E=H^{-1}\mathcal V$ is accessible as a subcategory of the simplicial arrow category. In particular there exist an infinite regular cardinal $\lambda$ in the input universe and a small set of arrows $E_0\subseteq E$ generating it under small $\lambda$-filtered colimits computed in that arrow category. This application uses the arbitrary-functor version of the inverse-image theorem, since $H$ need not be induced by an endpoint functor.

source.place: Agent derivation from the cited DAG statements; motivated by HTT Theorem 2.2.5.1, proof (1), and Corollary A.2.6.7

proof.text: For each $u\in E$, choose the small $\lambda$-filtered diagram of generators supplied by step 8. Every finite diagram has fewer than $\lambda$ morphisms, so its index category is filtered in the sense of the statement, including nonemptiness from the empty diagram. Thus this is already a small filtered presentation of $u$. If a presentation uses arrows only isomorphic to the chosen generators, choose isomorphisms $\alpha_d:D(d)\xrightarrow{\sim}e_d\in E_0$ and replace its transition square $D(a)$ by $\alpha_{d'}D(a)\alpha_d^{-1}$. The identity and composition equations follow by cancellation, and the $\alpha_d$ give an isomorphism of diagrams, hence of their colimits by the universal property. This yields precisely the asserted isomorphism in the arrow category. The argument does not require closure of $E$ under every filtered colimit or that the generators have finite endpoints.
